214	- `unparam` with check-exported fires on an unexported constructor whose field parameter always receives the same value, which will happen to every helper written ahead of the call sites that will vary it. 215	- `path.Clean` treats a backslash as an ordinary character, so a keyed path like `acme:skills\review` passes every containment check and produces a ref naming a file that exists on Windows and not on Linux. The grammar has to reject backslashes explicitly, ahead of cleaning; the absolute-path check has to run first so `C:\...` and `\\share\...` get the message about absolute paths instead.
216	- `path.Ext` treats a leading dot as the whole extension, so stripping unconditionally turns `.editorconfig` into an empty id. Only a non-empty remainder can replace the leaf.
217	- testifylint's useless-assert rejects `assert.Equal(t, f(), f())`, which is the obvious way to write 'this function returns a stable list'. Comparing both calls against a literal expected slice is what the linter wants and is a stronger assertion anyway, because it pins the order rather than only its stability.
218	- The Bash tool's working directory persists between calls, so a `cd` into a package directory silently rescopes a later `go test ./...` or `golangci-lint run ./...` to that package — which reports 0 issues and looks like a pass. Prefix repo-wide verification with an explicit cd to the repository root.
219	
220	### Iteration 10
221	
222	**Summary:** Added the manifest interpretation layer's defaulting half — the object override form, target defaulting and scope defaulting (Section 7, tasks 7.5–7.7) — taking the add-harnaas-foundation change from 44/74 to 47/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
223	
224	**Changes:**
225	- cmd/harnaas/cli/manifest/asset.go declares Scope (project/user) and Asset — one manifest entry with every question answered, where each field an entry may leave undeclared has already been inferred from its path or defaulted from the document, so a later phase cannot treat a declared `type` differently from an implied one
226	- ResolveType and ResolveID implement the object form's suppression rule one field at a time: a declared type is deliberately not checked against the path it overrides, because the object form exists precisely for a source whose layout does not follow the convention, and comparing them would refuse the case it was added for; a type outside harnaas's own vocabulary is still rejected, listing the five
227	- ResolveTargets returns the entry's own `targets` when declared and the manifest's `harnesses` otherwise, and returns a list of violations rather than one because `targets` is itself a list — each unrecognized name attributed to its own position (`assets[3].targets[0]`) so the aggregate orders identically on every run
228	- The nil-versus-empty Targets distinction decoding preserved is spent in ResolveTargets: an entry that declares nothing where the manifest declares no harnesses, and an entry that declares an empty list, both have nowhere to install but get different messages because they need different edits
229	- CheckHarnesses validates the document's own `harnesses` list once, at DocumentIndex with field `harnesses[1]`, so a misspelling there is one message rather than one per asset that inherited it; an empty list is deliberately not reported at document level, because it is only a problem for an asset that would have inherited it
230	- ResolveScope defaults to `project`, refuses a scope harnaas does not define, refuses `user` on an instruction pointing at `rule` as the type for that intent, and refuses `user` for any target the roster records no per-user location for — naming every offending target in one sentence and never falling back to project scope
231	- resolveScope takes the roster query as a parameter so the no-per-user-location refusal has a test today, when every harness on the roster has one; a target the roster does not know is skipped rather than reported twice, because the field that declared it already reported it
232	- violation.go generalizes assetSourceViolation into assetViolation(index, field, …), giving every per-field asset diagnostic the same `assets[N].<field>` spelling that the deterministic ordering in 7.9 sorts on
233	- Test coverage across an external file for the exported surface and an internal file for the roster seam: declared-beats-inferred in both directions, an unknown type, inherited and narrowed targets, both empty-effective-list cases, two unrecognized targets producing two positioned violations, the document-level harness list, the scope default in both entry forms, an undefined scope, user-on-an-instruction, and the four per-user-location branches including the plural sentence
234	- CLAUDE.md records the two load-bearing decisions — a default is inherited and checked once, and a wrong scope is refused rather than degraded — together with why the refusal needs a seam to be testable before the first harness without a per-user location is added
235	
236	**Learnings:**
237	- Validating an inherited default per asset would multiply one mistake by the number of entries that inherited it, so the manifest's `harnesses` list is checked once at DocumentIndex and ResolveTargets checks only what the entry itself declared. The consequence is that an inherited unrecognized name still reaches Asset.Targets — which is safe only because a document with any violation is never handed to a later phase, and that is now a load-bearing invariant rather than a convenience.
238	- Section 7.7's core rule is untestable against the real roster: claude-code is the only entry and it has PerUserLocation true, so there is no target for which `user` scope can be refused. Passing harness.HasPerUserLocation as a parameter to an unexported resolveScope — the same seam pattern jsonutil.writeFileAtomic already uses for its flush step — is what keeps the rule from rotting until the first harness that lacks a per-user location is added.
239	- A per-field violation helper has to produce a field name that sorts deterministically, which is why an unrecognized target is spelled `assets[3].targets[0]` rather than sharing one `assets[3].targets` field with its siblings. Lexical rather than numeric ordering of the bracketed index is a known and accepted consequence — 7.9 specifies ordering by index then field, and lexical field order is exactly that.
240	- gocritic's unlambda fires on a test closure that only forwards to the function it wraps, so a seam test wanting to pass the real implementation must pass the function value directly rather than wrapping it for readability; the explanatory comment has to move above the call site.
241	- Two test files for one source file is already the established convention here (jsonutil splits json_test.go external from write_test.go internal), so an exported-surface test in package manifest_test plus an internal test for the seam needs no justification beyond naming the internal one asset_internal_test.go.
242	- Task 7.8's aggregate is now the only thing standing between these resolvers and a usable interpretation entry point: every piece it needs (ParseSource, ParseAssetRef, CheckSourceKey, ResolveType, ResolveID, ResolveTargets, CheckHarnesses, ResolveScope) exists and returns Violations carrying index and field, so 7.8 is assembly plus the two cross-entry rules (duplicate ids within a type, unsafe id segments) rather than new interpretation.

**Learnings:**
- Logging cannot live under the project: task 8.11 requires that after init no .harnaas/ directory exists and harnaas.json is the only file that appeared, so the log file must go under os.UserCacheDir. Task 9.5's 'redirect home, cache and config under t.TempDir' harness confirms per-user state is where harnaas keeps everything that is not the manifest.

The uninitialised logger must also be a discarding logger rather than slog.Default(), which writes to stderr — a stray log call before Open would otherwise print.

### Iteration 5

**Summary:** Added the palette and jsonutil foundation packages (tasks 4.4 and 4.6) and routed the --json output path through jsonutil's canonical encoder, taking the add-harnaas-foundation change from 24/74 to 26/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.

**Changes:**
- cmd/harnaas/cli/palette is a zero-dependency package of base16 ANSI slot constants held as plain strings, so harnaas's colours are a request the terminal answers with the user's own theme rather than a hex value that is only correct on the machine it was picked on

- printJSON in cmd/harnaas/cli/output.go now encodes through jsonutil.Marshal and writes the finished bytes, so the --json document and the manifest init will write share one definition of the format, and an unencodable value returns an error with stdout still empty instead of a half-streamed document ahead of the entrypoint's error message
- Tasks 4.4 and 4.6 checked off in openspec/changes/add-harnaas-foundation/tasks.md; 4.7 left unchecked because its accessible-mode and piped-stream clauses depend on 4.5's uiform and interactive packages

**Learnings:**
- golangci-lint's std-error-handling exclusion preset already covers os.Remove and *.Close, so `_ = os.Remove(...)` and a deferred Close stay clean even with errcheck's check-blank: true — but Sync is not on that list, so the best-effort directory flush still needs an explicit nolint with a reason. This is the boundary that decides which dropped errors need a suppression and which do not.
- testifylint's encoded-compare rule rejects asserting an exact JSON string with assert.Equal and pushes toward assert.JSONEq, which would defeat a test whose whole subject is indentation and trailing newline. ### Iteration 6

**Summary:** Added the interactive and uiform foundation packages (tasks 4.5 and 4.7), completing Section 4 of the add-harnaas-foundation change and taking it from 26/74 to 28/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.

**Changes:**
- cmd/harnaas/cli/interactive resolves whether harnaas may prompt from the command's own streams plus the environment — HARNAAS_TEST_TTY override, then go test, then coding-agent sentinels (CLAUDECODE, CURSOR_AGENT, GEMINI_CLI, COPILOT_CLI, PI_CODING_AGENT), then CI, then both streams being terminals — with the decision biased towards 'no' because a flag-driven path always exists while a prompt shown to something that cannot answer hangs rather than degrades

- interactive.ShouldStyle is the single gate in front of the palette, honouring NO_COLOR and excluding TERM=cygwin, and is kept a separate question from CanPrompt because a run inside a coding agent must not be prompted and may still be styled
- Both decisions are split into pure cores (canPrompt, shouldStyle) taking getenv and the terminal answer as parameters, because `go test` can never present a real terminal and the exported functions would short-circuit before the environment gates were reached
- cmd/harnaas/cli/uiform is the only place harnaas builds a form, so accessible mode and the base16 theme are applied without anyone having to remember them; New takes explicit streams so prompts render on stderr and cannot corrupt a --json document on stdout
- uiform.Theme unsets the pinned foreground on titles and unselected options in both the focused and blurred variants so they inherit the terminal's default text colour, and points selection at palette.Accent — the theme declares no colour of its own
- uiform.Confirm returns ErrCancelled for a dismissed prompt rather than folding cancellation into a 'no', because the init spec requires a cancelled prompt to write nothing and exit non-zero while a decline is an ordinary answer
- uiform.Confirm consults the context directly before and after running the form, because huh reports a cancelled context as ErrTimeout and ignores the context entirely in accessible mode
- Test coverage: a table over every prompting gate including piped streams and the CI=false escape hatch, each agent sentinel individually, real os.Pipe and bytes.Buffer both answering 'not a terminal', the styling gates, accessible mode completing a prompt against non-terminal streams, cancellation reported separately from declining, and the theme's unstyled-titles and accent-selection guarantees

1	package manifest
2	
3	import (
4		"fmt"
5		"strconv"
6	)
7	
8	// DocumentIndex marks a violation belonging to the document as a whole rather
9	// than to one asset entry — a malformed `sources` value, an unrecognized name
10	// in `harnesses`.
11	//
12	// It is negative so it sorts ahead of every asset entry without a special case
13	// in the comparison: a problem with the whole document is the one an author
14	// should read first, because it is the one that can explain the entries below
15	// it.
16	const DocumentIndex = -1
17	
18	// Violation is one thing a decoded manifest says that harnaas cannot accept.
19	//
20	// Decoding stops at the first failure because a document that will not parse
21	// has no second problem to find. Interpretation does not stop: every asset entry
22	// is independent, so reporting one at a time would make a manifest with three
23	// mistakes three runs of the same command, each ending in a different sentence.
24	//
25	// A violation therefore carries where it is as data rather than only inside its
26	// sentence. That is what lets the aggregate order itself identically on every
27	// run — by [Violation.Index], then by [Violation.Field] — instead of inheriting
28	// the order a map happened to iterate in.
29	type Violation struct {
30		// Index is the asset entry's position in `assets`, or [DocumentIndex] for a
31		// violation about the document itself. It is the primary sort key.
32		Index int
33	
34		// Field names the part of the document at fault in the author's own
35		// vocabulary — `sources.acme`, `assets[2].scope` — so a reader knows which
36		// line to open, and so two violations on one entry order deterministically.
37		Field string
38	
39		// Problem states what is wrong, in one line.
40		Problem string
41	
42		// Fix states the exact edit that resolves it. It is always an edit for a
43		// person to make: harnaas does not write this file.
44		Fix string
45	}
46	
47	// String renders the location, the problem, a blank line, and the fix — the
48	// shape every user-facing diagnostic in harnaas takes.
49	//
50	// A violation is deliberately not an error. One of them is never what a command
51	// returns: interpretation collects them all and returns the aggregate, and a
52	// type that satisfied `error` would invite a caller to return the first one it
53	// saw, which is the behaviour accumulating exists to prevent.
54	func (v *Violation) String() string {
55		return fmt.Sprintf("%s: %s\n\n%s", v.Field, v.Problem, v.Fix)
56	}
57	
58	// sourceField names a `sources` entry, or the block itself where the entry has
59	// no key to be named by.
60	func sourceField(key string) string {
61		if key == "" {
62			return "sources"
63		}
64		return "sources." + key
65	}
66	
67	// assetField names an asset entry.
68	func assetField(index int) string {
69		return "assets[" + strconv.Itoa(index) + "]"
70	}
71	
72	// assetSubject is how every message refers to an asset entry.
73	//
74	// An entry has no other stable name: its id may be the thing that is wrong, and
75	// its source string may be absent. The index is the one thing an author can
76	// always count to in the file, so it is worth spelling identically everywhere,
77	// which is why both decoding and interpretation phrase it here.
78	func assetSubject(index int) string {
79		return fmt.Sprintf("the asset entry at index %d", index)
80	}
81	
82	// sourceViolation reports a problem with a `sources` entry.
83	func sourceViolation(key, problem, fix string) *Violation {
84		return &Violation{Index: DocumentIndex, Field: sourceField(key), Problem: problem, Fix: fix}
85	}

2	// which a project declares which harness assets it wants and where they come
3	// from.
4	//
5	// The package covers the manifest end to end in two layers that meet at
6	// [Document]. Decoding turns bytes into that document and interprets none of
7	// it: a field it accepts is one it could read, not one harnaas has agreed to.
8	// Interpretation then reads the document — parsing a source value, parsing an
9	// asset's source string, inferring a type and an id from a path, defaulting
10	// targets and scope, and checking the result against the harness roster.
11	//
12	// The two share one package because harnaas extracts a package only to break an
13	// import cycle, and there is none to break here: both layers are imported by
14	// the same callers, and splitting them would put the roster on one side of a
15	// boundary that exists for no other reason. What separates them instead is when
16	// they stop. Decoding stops at the first failure, because a document that will
17	// not parse has no second problem to find. Interpretation reports every
18	// violation at once as a [Violation] list, because every asset entry is
19	// independent and fixing three mistakes should not take three runs.
20	//
21	// # Strict decoding
22	//
23	// The manifest is written by a person and reviewed by a team, so an unknown
24	// field is nearly always a typo and surfacing it immediately is worth the cost
25	// of refusing to run. That is the whole test: strictness follows who writes the
26	// file, not what the file is called. `harnaas.lock.json` is machine-written and
27	// therefore decodes leniently, because a newer binary introduces fields an
28	// older binary would otherwise reject, bricking the file for everyone still on
29	// the older version.
30	//
31	// The version field is what bounds that trade. It is read on its own, ahead of
32	// the strict pass, so a manifest written by a newer harnaas is refused with an
33	// explicit "upgrade harnaas" message rather than a confusing complaint about
34	// the first field this binary happens not to know.
35	//
36	// A decode failure returns no document at all. Half a manifest is not a smaller
37	// manifest — it is a different one, and installing from it would place a subset
38	// of what the project declared while reporting success.

45	// remedy this package reports is therefore phrased as the exact edit for a
46	// person to make, never as a command that would make it for them. A test over
47	// this package's own sources asserts no write call has crept in.
48	package manifest

50	// FileName is the manifest's only accepted name, at the repository root.
51	//

53	// declaration: a `--manifest` pointing somewhere else would mean two developers
54	// in the same repository could install different asset sets and both be right.

57	// SupportedVersion is the manifest schema version this binary understands.
58	//
59	// A manifest declaring a greater version is refused with an upgrade message
60	// rather than read partially, because the fields this binary would silently
61	// ignore are exactly the ones the newer harnaas added to change what the
62	// document means.

70	// them. An empty field here means "not declared", never "declared as the

An asset's `scope` SHALL default to `project`. `user` scope SHALL be accepted only for a target
harness the harness roster records as having an unambiguous per-user location; declaring it for any

## Purpose

Defines `harnaas.json`, the committed, hand-edited file in which a project declares which harness
assets it wants and where they come from. It covers the file's location, its strict decoding, the
document shape, the `sources` block, how each asset's type and id are inferred from its path, target

The manifest SHALL be a single file named `harnaas.json` at the repository root, resolved from the
project root carried in the request context so it is found from any subdirectory. A `harnaas.json`
discovered in a subdirectory of the project SHALL be a validation error naming the root manifest as
the only one harnaas reads. When the root has no manifest, a command requiring one SHALL say so and
name `harnaas init`.

#### Scenario: Manifest found from a subdirectory

- **WHEN** a command runs in a nested directory of a project whose root contains `harnaas.json`

would otherwise reject, bricking the file with no fix available to the user who hits it. That test,
not the filename, is why `harnaas.json` is strict and `harnaas.lock.json` is lenient.

key_changes_made: cmd/harnaas/cli/manifest/interpret.go adds Interpret(doc), the second layer's whole entry point: it parses every `sources` value, checks the document's harness list once, interprets every asset entry, and returns an *Interpretation carrying the document, the parsed sources and the resolved assets — or nothing at all, which is how 'a document with any violation is never handed to a later phase' is enforced rather than merely stated, since Interpret is the only route to an Asset

interpretEntry accumulates within an entry instead of returning at its first problem, but declines to ask a question whose answer would have to be invented: where the source string did not parse there is no path to infer a type or an id from, so inference is skipped unless the entry declared the field itself, while targets and every declared field are still checked

manifest.ValidationError in errors.go is the aggregate: file, problem count in the singular or plural, then every violation in the problem-then-fix shape, with Violations exposed already ordered so a caller rendering them itself sees what the message would have shown

sortViolations orders by asset index then field, putting document-level problems first through DocumentIndex being negative, so two runs over one manifest produce byte-identical output despite `sources` decoding into a map

interpret_test.go adds the documented example manifest as a fixture that decodes strictly and interprets clean with every field asserted, a manifest with six independent violations asserting the exact reported order, a twenty-run determinism check over a four-key sources block, both halves of the per-type uniqueness rule, a table over every accepted and rejected id spelling, the aggregate's own rendering in both the singular and plural, and a re-assertion that no remedy offers a command

The 'never handed to a later phase' rule is only enforceable if the interpreted type is unreachable without the check. Returning ([]Asset, error) and letting callers ignore the error would leave the rule as documentation; returning a single *Interpretation that is nil on any violation makes it structural, and is why the type exists at all rather than Interpret returning the pieces separately.

A malformed `sources` value would otherwise produce two violations for one mistake — the bad value, and every asset 'referencing an undeclared key'. Registering the key with a zero Source when its value fails to parse keeps CheckSourceKey satisfied, because the key genuinely is declared; only its value is not.

Skipping type and id inference when the source string failed to parse is what stops one bad asset string from producing three violations, since InferType and InferID would both run against an empty path. The guard is `refParsed || entry.<field> != ""`, which keeps a declared field checked even when the path it would have overridden is unusable.

Every violation constructor already carried its index and field as data from iterations 9 and 10, so 7.9's determinism requirement was one slices.SortStableFunc over (Index, Field) with no changes to any producer — the design decision that made this cheap was made two iterations before it paid off.

Sections 8 (init) and 9 (guardrail tests) are now the only implementation work left, and neither depends on Interpret: init writes a scaffold and never reads assets, so the interpretation layer has no caller in this change and will first be exercised by add-harnaas-install.
